title: Grace (ST I-II.109–114)
hookLine: we need God's help both to know and to do the good fully

lines: A COUCH STUCK IN THE DOORWAY.
cards: A couch is wedged in a doorway, one arm through, one arm stuck. The person moving it has pushed, lifted, tilted. It isn't that they're weak.

They got it down the hall alone, and up the porch steps. But there's a point where one person, however strong, can't finish the job. Then a neighbor walks by, grabs the other end, says pivot, and the couch slides through.
If the light of right and wrong is already on in us, is the light enough? Thomas's answer is grace.

teach.b: Thomas opens his treatise on grace with a careful question: what can a person do without it? The answer is not nothing. People can know many true things by the natural light of the mind.
Even after the fall, they can do some particular goods by their own powers. His examples are wonderfully ordinary: building houses, planting vineyards. Then the turn.

teach.h: SOME GOOD IS NOT THE WHOLE GOOD.
teach.b: Some good is not the whole good. Thomas compares fallen human nature to a sick person who can move around a little, but can't move freely until medicine heals him. So grace does two jobs.
It heals what's wounded, and it lifts us toward a good beyond our nature: friendship with God, the charity of three days ago. No amount of pushing gets the couch through that door alone.
Even turning toward God in the first place, even getting ready for grace, is itself God's help at work.
Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "For it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will." And Jesus, in John: "without me you can do nothing."
One line from the very start of the Summa keeps this from sounding grim: grace does not destroy nature, Thomas says, but perfects it. Grace isn't God shoving us aside to do the job himself.

teach.h: WITHOUT ME YOU CAN DO NOTHING.
teach.b: It's the other end of the couch. Back on day three hundred eight, it was free, not earned. Justice, fortitude, temperance, charity: each is something a person grows in.
Today Thomas names the help underneath them.

how: Catholics speak of grace as God's free gift, received especially through prayer and the sacraments, and the Church teaches that even the first turning toward God is moved by grace.

o: a reward God hands out for good behavior
God's free help that heals and lifts our nature
a feeling of calm that comes with prayer

games.q: grace, by Thomas — tap the pairs.
p: good people can do on their own
can move a little, not freely

s: Thomas says people can do no good at all without grace
he names building houses and planting vineyards. some good, yes; the whole good, no.
for Thomas, even getting ready for grace is God's help at work
turning toward God in the first place is already moved by God.
Thomas says grace destroys our nature and replaces it
grace does not destroy nature, he says, but perfects it.

games.q: can a person do any good at all without grace? what does Thomas answer?
o: some particular goods, but not the whole good.
all the good there is, unaided.
games.why: Thomas says people can build houses and plant vineyards, but need grace to heal and lift them toward the whole good.

practice: Pick the next real task in front of you, a hard email, a meal to cook, a conversation, a shift at work, and notice honestly, without shame, where your own strength runs out in it.
If you pray, ask God for help with that task before you start, in your own words or a prayer you know; if you don't, think of one person you could ask, and let yourself be willing.

wordCard.voice: Grace. For Thomas, God's free help, which heals human nature and lifts it toward a good beyond its reach, without destroying it. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, the word Paul uses for grace: favor, a gift freely given.

carryVoice: Your line: help is needed. Asking isn't weakness; it's taking the other end. I'll be here tomorrow.
